variants.title: Start from the deployment constraint
variants.context: Compression starts from a deployment constraint, not from a technique: name the binding constraint, profile the baseline, choose a technique the backend can execute, export the real artifact, then evaluate and canary it.
variants.prompt: A mobile team is told the model must fit a smaller device package. Put the compression steps in order.

items.text: Choose a compatible technique: match precision, sparsity, architecture, and operator changes to kernels the backend can execute.
Evaluate and canary: compare quality slices and system metrics with the baseline, then expand only while gates hold.
Name the binding constraint: state the package size, memory, cold start, latency, throughput, power, or cost target.
Export the real artifact: pin the recipe, calibration set, operator graph, packing, compiler, runtime, device, and integrity.
Profile the baseline: measure weights, activations, caches, workspace, operators, bandwidth, and non-model request stages.

variants.hint: One step decides which number the whole project is trying to move.
variants.explanation: Compression is useful only in relation to a target system, so the binding constraint and a baseline profile come before any technique.

variants.title: Start from the deployment constraint
variants.context: Compression starts from a deployment constraint, not from a technique: name the binding constraint, profile the baseline, choose a technique the backend can execute, export the real artifact, then evaluate and canary it.
variants.prompt: A serving team wants lower p99 latency and proposes 4-bit weights immediately. Put the steps in order to test that idea.

items.text: Profile the baseline: find whether time is spent in weights, activations, memory movement, batching, or non-model stages.
Choose a compatible technique: adopt 4-bit only if the backend has kernels for it at the required shapes.
Export the real artifact: lower the graph with pinned packing, compiler, runtime, and device identifiers.
Evaluate and canary: measure latency percentiles and quality slices against the baseline before expanding traffic.
Name the binding constraint: state p99 latency under the real request mix rather than artifact size.

variants.hint: Profiling can show that the proposed change does not touch the bottleneck.
variants.explanation: A technique is chosen after the baseline profile identifies where the constraint actually binds, because storage reduction need not move latency at all.

variants.title: Start from the deployment constraint
variants.context: Compression starts from a deployment constraint, not from a technique: name the binding constraint, profile the baseline, choose a technique the backend can execute, export the real artifact, then evaluate and canary it.
variants.prompt: Cold start on a serverless endpoint is the complaint. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Export the real artifact: pin the compiled graph, weight format, runtime, and device the endpoint will load.
Evaluate and canary: measure cold and warm behavior together, then expand only while both stay inside their gates.
Name the binding constraint: define cold start under the real invocation pattern and package limits.
Profile the baseline: separate download, load, first-run compilation, and warm inference in the measured startup path.
Choose a compatible technique: pick a transformation that shrinks the stage that actually dominates startup.

variants.hint: The stage that dominates startup is not always the one holding the weights.
variants.explanation: Profiling the end-to-end system first is what stops a team from compressing a component that was never the constraint.

variants.title: Compose transformations reproducibly
variants.context: Techniques interact, so they are composed in a reproducible order: freeze the baseline, apply one transformation and measure it alone, recover quality, export after the final change, then compare against every baseline.
variants.prompt: A team plans to prune and then quantize the same model. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Apply one transformation: record the pruning recipe and measure its isolated effect before adding quantization.
Export after the final change: evaluate the graph and weights the runtime will load, not an intermediate framework object.
Compare with every baseline: attribute gains and losses per step and preserve a simpler fallback.
Freeze the baseline: pin the source model, data, evaluation, serving runtime, and the baseline quality and performance report.
Recover quality: fine-tune with representative data, keeping masks, hyperparameters, and calibration statistics versioned.

variants.hint: Attribution is only possible while one thing has changed at a time.
variants.explanation: Composing transformations without isolating them makes a regression impossible to attribute and a fragile combination impossible to reject.

variants.title: Compose transformations reproducibly
variants.context: Techniques interact, so they are composed in a reproducible order: freeze the baseline, apply one transformation and measure it alone, recover quality, export after the final change, then compare against every baseline.
variants.prompt: A distilled student will also be quantized for the edge build. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Export after the final change: lower the quantized student and evaluate that artifact rather than the training object.
Compare with every baseline: report the student against the teacher and the quantized student against the student.
Apply one transformation: quantize the student alone and record the exact format, granularity, and calibration manifest.
Recover quality: recalibrate or fine-tune with representative data and version the statistics that were used.
Freeze the baseline: pin the teacher, the student recipe, and the uncompressed student's measured quality and latency.

variants.hint: There is more than one baseline once two transformations are stacked.
variants.explanation: Each transform creates a new artifact needing its own evaluation, so every stacked result is compared against each earlier baseline.

variants.title: Compose transformations reproducibly
variants.context: Techniques interact, so they are composed in a reproducible order: freeze the baseline, apply one transformation and measure it alone, recover quality, export after the final change, then compare against every baseline.
variants.prompt: After recovery fine-tuning, a pruned model's sparsity has quietly disappeared. Put the steps in order to rebuild the run.

items.text: Apply one transformation: reapply the pruning recipe and record the resulting structure explicitly.
Freeze the baseline: return to the pinned source model, data, and serving runtime that the report was written against.
Export after the final change: confirm the sparsity survives export, constant folding, and backend lowering.
Compare with every baseline: show the isolated effect of pruning before claiming any combined result.
Recover quality: fine-tune with masks or parameterizations enforced so the removed structure cannot refill.

variants.hint: Ask at which step the removed structure could come back.
variants.explanation: Fine-tuning can undo sparsity unless masks are enforced, and export can fold it away, so the structure is verified in the artifact the runtime loads.

variants.title: Compute weight storage
variants.context: Theoretical weight storage is parameters times the retained fraction times bits divided by 8. Production memory also includes scales, activations, caches, workspaces, and reserve, so this number is a floor and not a runtime budget.
variants.prompt: A 3 billion parameter model is quantized to 8-bit weights with no pruning. What is the theoretical weight storage of the compressed artifact?
variants.hint: Convert bits to bytes before reading the total.
variants.explanation: 3 billion parameters times 1.0 retained times 8 bits divided by 8 is 3 GB of weights, before scales, metadata, activations, and workspace.

mistakes.feedback: That leaves the answer in bits, since dividing by 8 is what converts to bytes.
That is the FP32 baseline at 32 bits per parameter, not the quantized artifact.

variants.title: Compute weight storage
variants.context: Theoretical weight storage is parameters times the retained fraction times bits divided by 8. Production memory also includes scales, activations, caches, workspaces, and reserve, so this number is a floor and not a runtime budget.
variants.prompt: A 4 billion parameter model keeps 50 percent of its weights after structured pruning and is then stored at 4 bits. What is the theoretical weight storage?
variants.hint: Both the retained fraction and the bit width shrink the same payload.
variants.explanation: 4 billion times 0.5 retained times 4 bits divided by 8 is 1 GB of weights, which is a storage floor rather than a runtime memory budget.

mistakes.feedback: That ignores the retained fraction and prices every original parameter.
That counts bits as bytes, skipping the division by 8.

variants.title: Compute weight storage
variants.context: Theoretical weight storage is parameters times the retained fraction times bits divided by 8. Production memory also includes scales, activations, caches, workspaces, and reserve, so this number is a floor and not a runtime budget.
variants.prompt: A 7 billion parameter model keeps 80 percent of its weights and is stored at 16 bits. What is the theoretical weight storage?
variants.hint: Apply the retained fraction to the parameter count first.
variants.explanation: 7 billion times 0.8 retained times 16 bits divided by 8 is 11.2 GB, and the runtime still adds activations, caches, workspace, and reserve.

mistakes.feedback: That prices the full parameter count and ignores the 20 percent that was removed.
That uses 8 bits per parameter instead of the 16 bits the artifact actually stores.

variants.title: Diagnose the compressed artifact
variants.context: A mathematically smaller model can run at the same speed or slower. The exported artifact is the thing that must improve a declared constraint, and only a measurement of that artifact on the target backend counts as evidence.
variants.prompt: A model is pruned to 60 percent sparsity and quality holds, but latency on the target backend is unchanged. Inspection shows the exported graph carries dense tensors of the original shape with many zeros. What is the finding?
options: Unstructured zeros still execute through dense kernels, so nothing about the runtime work actually changed.
The sparsity ratio is too low to matter, so pushing it to 85 percent should finally reduce latency.
Quality was preserved because recovery fine-tuning restored the weights that pruning had removed.
optionFeedback: Correct: unstructured sparsity reduces logical density but needs structured removal or specialized execution to reduce time.
More zeros in the same dense tensors produce the same dense work, so the ratio is not the obstacle.
Refilled weights would change the sparsity report, and the graph still shows the zeros that were introduced.
variants.hint: Ask what shape the runtime actually multiplies.
variants.explanation: Only structure the runtime can exploit changes measured latency, so pruning is checked in the exported graph and against the kernels that will execute it.

variants.title: Diagnose the compressed artifact
variants.context: A mathematically smaller model can run at the same speed or slower. The exported artifact is the thing that must improve a declared constraint, and only a measurement of that artifact on the target backend counts as evidence.
variants.prompt: A report shows 41 percent latency improvement measured on the eager framework model, while production loads a compiled artifact from a separate export step. What should the reviewer require?
options: Accept the number for the latency gate and verify only quality on the exported artifact.
Rerun the benchmark on the exported artifact in its serving runtime, since that is what production executes.
Accept the number and apply a fixed discount, since compiled artifacts are normally faster than eager execution.
optionFeedback: Splitting the evidence still leaves the latency claim resting on a configuration nobody ships.
Correct: the source checkpoint is not the production artifact, so evidence must come from the graph the runtime loads.
An invented discount is not a measurement, and lowering can be slower when operators fall back.
variants.hint: Which object will the serving process actually load?
variants.explanation: Evaluating a framework model while deploying a separately lowered artifact is a named trap, because export and lowering change both speed and numerics.

variants.title: Diagnose the compressed artifact
variants.context: A mathematically smaller model can run at the same speed or slower. The exported artifact is the thing that must improve a declared constraint, and only a measurement of that artifact on the target backend counts as evidence.
variants.prompt: A compressed candidate keeps average accuracy within 0.3 points of the baseline, but a required low-resource language slice falls 6 points and a safety classifier proxy drops sharply. What should the gate do?
options: Promote and add the slice to the next release's monitoring so the trend can be watched.
Block promotion, since a required slice regression is not offset by a stable aggregate.
Promote with a smaller canary, since the aggregate shows the artifact is broadly healthy.
optionFeedback: Monitoring after promotion converts a measured failure into an incident waiting to be observed.
Correct: average retention can hide concentrated harm, so required slices are gated separately from the aggregate.
A smaller canary reduces exposure but still ships a known regression to the affected population.
variants.hint: Who is inside the slice that moved?
variants.explanation: Compression harms are usually concentrated, so required slices carry their own floors and an aggregate cannot waive them.

variants.title: Map each part to its job
variants.context: Compression is a family of transformations with distinct mechanisms, sparsity patterns with distinct runtime consequences, and a manifest whose sections each pin a different part of the released artifact's identity.
variants.prompt: Match each compression technique to what it changes.

pairs.label: Quantization
pairs.detail: Represents weights or activations with fewer bits under granularity, scale, and backend rules.

pairs.label: Pruning
pairs.detail: Removes weights, blocks, channels, heads, or layers from the existing model.

pairs.label: Distillation
pairs.detail: Trains a separate student model against labels plus teacher signals.

pairs.label: Factorization
pairs.detail: Approximates large matrices with smaller factors whose rank controls the trade-off.

variants.hint: Ask whether the technique edits the model, its numbers, or replaces it with a new one.
variants.explanation: Each technique changes a different part of the system, so their evidence and their failure modes do not substitute for one another.

variants.title: Map each part to its job
variants.context: Compression is a family of transformations with distinct mechanisms, sparsity patterns with distinct runtime consequences, and a manifest whose sections each pin a different part of the released artifact's identity.
variants.prompt: Match each sparsity choice to its runtime consequence.

pairs.label: Unstructured zeros
pairs.detail: Reduce logical density while still executing through ordinary dense kernels.

pairs.label: N:M pattern sparsity
pairs.detail: Can map to supported sparse hardware when dimensions and kernels match.

pairs.label: Structured removal
pairs.detail: Changes dense tensor shapes, so ordinary dense work actually shrinks.

pairs.label: Recovery fine-tuning
pairs.detail: Lets remaining capacity adapt, and still needs independent evaluation afterwards.

variants.hint: Ask which of these changes the shape the kernel multiplies.
variants.explanation: Pruning pays off only where the runtime can exploit the structure, which is why the pattern is chosen against the backend rather than the metric.

variants.title: Map each part to its job
variants.context: Compression is a family of transformations with distinct mechanisms, sparsity patterns with distinct runtime consequences, and a manifest whose sections each pin a different part of the released artifact's identity.
variants.prompt: Match each manifest section to what it pins.

pairs.label: Source identity
pairs.detail: Checkpoint, architecture, preprocessing, transformation order, recipes, code, and seeds.

pairs.label: Data identity
pairs.detail: Calibration, recovery, teacher-output, and evaluation datasets with sampling and privacy rules.

pairs.label: Runtime identity
pairs.detail: Exported graph, weight format, operator set, compiler, backend, device, driver, and serving config.

pairs.label: Evidence identity
pairs.detail: Slice metrics, latency distributions, memory, cost, canary results, approval, and rollback target.

variants.hint: Ask what a reviewer could not reconstruct if the section were missing.
variants.explanation: A complete manifest is what separates a reproducible compressed release from two artifacts that merely share a name.
